html:
The siege of Xiangyang lasted from 1267 to 1273 at the twin cities of Xiangyang and Fancheng, on the Han River in today's Hubei province, central China. The Mongol armies of Kublai Khan took both cities from the Southern Song dynasty.

The Song had held off the Mongols for more than thirty years. The two fortresses faced each other across the Han River and blocked the way down to the Yangtze and the rich south. They had wide moats and strong walls, and were supplied by boat. Cavalry was of little use, so the Mongols built forts around them and a river fleet to cut the supply line. In the end Kublai sent to his nephew in Persia for two Muslim engineers, who built counterweight trebuchets that threw far heavier stones than Chinese machines. Fancheng was stormed early in 1273. After a few shots hit Xiangyang, its commander Lü Wenhuan surrendered.

The road south was open. The Song capital Hangzhou fell in 1276, and the last Song court was destroyed in 1279. Kublai's Yuan dynasty then ruled all of China. It was a high point of the Mongol conquests.
